articles.title: Anti-migrant protesters scuffle with police in Gosport after Channel rescue
articles.summary:
Demonstrators gather in south coast town as nearly 150 people trying to reach UK by small boat brought ashore

Anti-migrant protesters have scuffled with police in Gosport, Hampshire, as they…

blocks.text: Anti-migrant protesters have scuffled with police in Gosport, Hampshire, as they opposed the rescuing of nearly 150 people trying to reach the UK by small boat.

The demonstrators gathered in the south coast town as news of the vessel’s expected arrival spread. It was the second time protesters had targeted the town amid rumours of rescued people disembarking there.
Several rescued people were seen arriving at a marina in Gosport after being transported onboard two RNLI boats late on Sunday evening.
Their dinghy was shadowed by French rescue vessels while in the Channel until it was met by RNLI boats in English waters, according to ship tracking data.

The Home Office said 149 migrants were believed to be onboard. It said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to protect our border. We have established contingency plans to make sure we can securely disembark, check and process all small boat arrivals. Migrants will be transported to short term holding facilities in Kent where they will be processed as normal and undergo stringent health, security and biometric checks.”

On Sunday, Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said it had deployed officers to Gosport to “support our partners in the event of an emergency at sea”. Ambulances and coaches were also spotted in the area.
The force imposed conditions under the Public Order Act as well as powers prohibiting the wearing of face coverings.
Demonstrators had assembled near Haslar Marina where the atmosphere was mostly peaceful, though there were reports of flares being set off and some scuffles with police.
There were similar scenes last month when protesters gathered in the area expecting migrants to arrive on a dinghy, but they were ultimately taken to Dover by sea.

Departures so far west have been rare in recent years, but it is the third such crossing in a month. In September, British rescue boats collected passengers of a dinghy that had spent around 30 hours at sea after setting off from Normandy. The 51 people, who refused help from the French coastguard, arrived in Dover after being transferred to Border Security Command boats.
after newsletter promotion
It was expected they would be taken to Gosport, with hundreds of protesters gathering after coaches and ambulances were spotted in the area. Six people were arrested by officers during that evening.
The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451. This is down 43% on this time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024.

blocks.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called an early general election on Monday, bringing forward a vote that had been scheduled for 2027.
Sanchez announced the decision in a statement at Madrid's Moncloa Palace after a weekend of consultations with his closest advisers.
What did Sanchez say?
"It is time for Spaniards to decide what future you want," Sanchez said.
The announcement of the November 29 vote follows a parliamentary defeat for his minority government on Friday, when lawmakers rejected measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis.

Sanchez framed the election as a choice over Spain's future direction, saying voters must decide whether the country joins what he called a "far-right wave" or continues on a path of "openness, social justice and environmental responsibility."
He said he trusted Spanish voters to make that choice.
The decision comes despite Sanchez repeatedly insisting in recent months that his government would complete its four-year term.
The election follows mounting public pressure over housing costs, with large protests across the country.

articles.title: Shadow chancellor to address Tory conference as he claims slashing red tape could cut cost of new houses by £50,000 – UK politics live
articles.summary: Andrew Griffith makes speech today as Reform UK accuses party of copying policies they ‘announced weeks and months ago’

blocks.text: Good morning. Yesterday Kemi Badenoch published a tract setting out the principles that a Conservative government would follow in office. It was presented as Thatcherism revived for the 21st century, and a key theme was that government should leave wealth creation up to business, and not get in the way with red tape.

Today Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, is presenting a plan that illustrates what this would mean in practice. Normally, at party conference, ministers and shadow ministers put out a press release in advance of their speeches highlighting just one headline policy idea, with perhaps one or two associated policies.

Overnight Griffith has published what is practically a manifesto. The press release alone runs to almost 5,000 words. Jessica Elgot had the task of reading them all for us yesterday and here is her write-up.
She has led her story on the plan to get rid of two environment quangos, the Environment Agency and Natural England.
But there are plenty of other proposals in the package too, including:
-Getting rid of net zero regulations and other planning laws, including section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy, that put up the cost of housebuilding.
-Getting rid of the EPR (extended producer responsibility), a law intended to make producers liable for waste disposal costs. The Tories call it the “grocery tax”.
-Backing a third runway at Heathrow.

-Leaving the Aarhus convention, an international treaty giving the public access to information relating to environmental decision-making. The Tories claim this enables the “lawfare hindering every major infrastructure project in this country”.
-Speeding up the delivery of more nuclear power stations.
-Simplifying the tax code.
The Tories claim the plans relating to housebuilding would “cut up to an estimated £50,000 off the price of a new home”.
There is more detail in what Griffith is proposing, and there is clearly a lot to discuss. Labour and Reform UK have both responded overnight – but taking different lines of attack.
Labour has said that Griffith has no credibility on these topics. In an overnight statement, Bridget Phillipson, the party chair, said:

double quotation markTrusting the co-author of Liz Truss’ disastrous mini-Budget with Tory plans on the economy and housing is like asking an arsonist to run the fire service. Kemi Badenoch is once again demonstrating her appalling lack of judgement. The Tories had 14 years in government to grow our economy and help people get on the housing ladder, but they completely failed at every turn.
But Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader and business spokesperson, says that Griffith is copying ideas that his party has already adopted. He says:

double quotation markTories pledge to scrap some costs regulations and taxes they put in place! They are copying Reform policies we announced weeks and months ago! They are trying to fix problems they created 😡 Never forget Never forgive

One of the themes emerging at this conference is that, while there is far less talk of some sort of Tory/Reform UK pact than there was a year ago, the policy overlap continues. Yesterday the Conservatives announced two other proposals (excluding foreigners from the student loan scheme, and reducing aid spending to just £1bn a year) that were little more than cut-and-paste versions of Reform UK pledges.
Here is the agenda for the day.

9.45am: Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, speaks at the conference on the main stage (the smaller of the two halls the Tories are using at this conference for speeches). The other main morning speakers are Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, at 10.30am; Damian Hinds, the shadow health secretary, at 11.15am; and Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, and Laura Trott, after 12.15pm.
12.14pm: Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, speaking in the fanzone area on the Conservative’s rural vision.

2pm: Griffith takes part in “meet the team” event in the symphony hall (the conference stage being used for larger events) with Richard Fuller, chief secretary to the Treasury, Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, and Julia Lopez, the acting shadow business secretary.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

“Customer loyalty is key to the PLDT Group’s long-term growth,” according to Menardo G. Jimenez, Jr., PLDT Chief Operating Officer. “As PLDT and Smart customer expectations evolve, we must strengthen our relationship with them, deepen engagement through our products and services, and deliver greater value throughout the customer journey. By investing in customer loyalty through our collaboration with Capillary, we are investing in stronger customer retention, sustainable growth, and the PLDT Group’s continued industry leadership.”

It’s our way of saying thank you while making every interaction with PLDT Home more valuable, more engaging, and more rewarding,” said John Y. Palanca, Head of PLDT Home.

Manaloto, officer-in-charge of Smart. articles.title: BT to buy broadband supplier TalkTalk, saving 900 jobs
articles.summary: UK’s fourth-biggest broadband provider has been seeking a buyer for several years

blocks.text: BT has agreed to buy the broadband supplier TalkTalk out of administration in a rescue deal that will save 900 jobs.
The company said it had struck a deal to acquire TalkTalk and its wholesale business PlatformX Communications (PXC) on a debt-free basis, in a move that is expected to cost it £400m.

The secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, Lisa Nandy, intervened ⁠on ⁠Monday after the acquisition ⁠was confirmed, citing risks to public ⁠services and ​vulnerable customers ‌if TalkTalk’s broadband ‌services were disrupted.

Her department said it was acting under Enterprise ‌Act powers, allowing Nandy to consider the wider public interest once the Competition and ​Markets Authority has reported back by 19 October on any competition concerns raised by the tie-up.
BT said the deal will “protect continuity of service for its [TalkTalk’s] 2.5 million customers, avoiding the risk of material harm to vulnerable customers and key emergency services”.

It said it expected to report a £400m cash hit from the deal in its current financial year, comprising transaction and administration costs, working capital, as well as a £60m trading loss and £100m in uncollected Openreach revenue.
Allison Kirkby, the chief executive of BT, said it was “a genuinely unprecedented situation, where millions of citizens and businesses were at risk if TalkTalk had collapsed”.
“Our immediate priority is to stabilise the business and provide a safety net for the households and businesses who rely on TalkTalk.”

TalkTalk, which is the UK’s fourth biggest broadband company, has struggled in a highly competitive telecoms market, with its retail customer numbers dwindling from 4 million in 2019 to about 1.5 million this year.

Its founder, Charles Dunstone, engineered a £1.1bn deal with the London-based hedge fund Toscafund in 2021 to take the company private, which saddled the business with debt. Since then it has, in effect, been under the control of its lenders, led by the US private credit group Ares Management.
The deal with BT ends Dunstone’s prolonged efforts to sell TalkTalk, although the agreement is expected to trigger a regulatory review over the coming weeks.
after newsletter promotion
Administrators at Alvarez & Marsal Europe said the sale would transfer all 900 employees at TalkTalk’s consumer and broadband business and PXC to BT.

BT is the biggest broadband provider in the UK, with a market share of about 30%, according to estimates by Enders Analysis. Openreach, the broadband network owned by BT, is also TalkTalk’s biggest supplier. BT can expect to add a further 1.5 million broadband customers as a result of the deal.
The companies will operate separately and continue to compete until the regulatory review is over, BT said in a statement.
TalkTalk, which is headquartered in Salford, reported revenues of about £1.2bn over the past 12 months and was loss-making, BT said.

articles.title: China denies giving money to Philippine political group in wake of Trillanes' claims
articles.summary: In a statement that didn't name the Philippine parties involved, spokesman Ji Lingpeng said the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines has noted that certain Philippine politicians fabricated and spread…

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 2:55pm
The Chinese Embassy in Manila has branded as a "false narrative" the allegations that China has funneled funds to a political faction in the Philippines, calling them "malicious rhetoric and actions"

Chinese Embassy spokesperson Ji Lingpeng said this days after former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV claimed that Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, lawyer Maneses Carpio, accepted P150 million and P319 million from China through separate organizations.

In a statement that didn't name the Philippine parties involved, Ji said the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines has noted that certain Philippine politicians fabricated and spread a false narrative alleging that China had funneled funds to a particular political faction in the Philippines.
The statement also referred to an allegation that the Chinese Embassy’s website had been maliciously linked to as a redirect destination.

"We strongly condemn and firmly oppose such malicious rhetoric and actions. We urge the relevant individuals in the Philippines to stop political manipulation and not to drag Philippine domestic politics into China-Philippines relations," Ji said.

"Attempts to achieve personal political gains by smearing and discrediting China and harming China's interests and image are doomed to fail and will ultimately undermine the interests of the Philippines and its people," he added.
Sara Duterte's spokesman Atty. Paolo Panelo over the weekend branded as "malicious fabrications" Trillanes' allegations, which were presented in a news conference on Friday.

"Because of these repeated, unmasked deceptions, the Filipino people have rightfully and overwhelmingly rejected Trillanes in every subsequent attempt to get elected back into public office," Panelo said.
Ji said the Chinese Embassy would "take all necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate interests and dignity."

In a statement on Saturday, Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro said allegations that Sara Duterte and her husband Mans Carpio received money from the Chinese government raised "serious implications for national security."
Teodoro urged Trillanes to submit evidence, so it could be "thoroughly investigated."

"The allegations of Fmr. Senator Trillanes, if substantiated, raise serious implications for national security. He should submit the evidence in his possession, if any, to our law enforcement authorities so the matter can be thoroughly investigated," Teodoro said.
On Friday, Malacañang lambasted officials who remained silent on territorial issues like the West Philippine Sea, especially those who accepted bribes to do so.
Without naming names, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro did not mince words when asked about former senator Antonio Trillanes’ claim of Chinese money making its way to Sara Duterte and Mans Carpio.

“Kung sapat ang ebidensya, hindi ito dapat isawalang-bahala. Maituturing na pagtataksil sa bayan ang mga Filipino lalo na kung sila ay mga public official na kaya pala tahimik sa mga karahasang natatanggap ng iba nating mangingisda sa kamay ng mga dayuhan, at ang iba naman ay handang ipamigay ang parte ng ating teritoryo o karapatan sa WPS ay dahil natatapalan ng pera ang kanilang mga mata para talikuran ang pagmamahal sa sariling bayan at ibenta ang ating kalayaan,” Castro said in a message to reporters.

(If the evidence is sufficient, then this should not be brushed aside. Filipinos, especially public officials, are guilty of betraying the country if they are silent on the violence faced by our fisherfolks in the hands of foreigners, with some of them even ready to give away parts of the WPS because they were blinded by money to forget their love of the nation and sell out freedom.) –NB, GMA News

articles.title: 91 of Bato dela Rosa's 117 firearms still unaccounted for -- PNP
articles.summary: Ninety-one of the 117 firearms registered to Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa remain unaccounted for, while 26 have so far been turned in, the Philippine National Police (PNP) said Monday.

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 2:51pm
Ninety-one of the 117 firearms registered to Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa remain unaccounted for, while 26 have so far been turned in, the Philippine National Police (PNP) said Monday.
At a press briefing, PNP Civil Security Group (CSG) director Major General Aden Lagradante said the PNP was still accounting for the remaining firearms.
“Hindi pa. Ninety-one from 117. Twenty-six yung turned in, so we still have 91,” Lagradante said.
Lagradante said the PNP was continuing to coordinate with the senator’s legal officer regarding the remaining firearms.
He said dela Rosa’s camp had also sought reconsideration of the matter through the Firearms and Explosives Office (FEO).
“Sa ngayon, administratively revoked yung license niya. By our rules, dapat ma-surrender, but ang last na information is on the process of accounting doon sa mga remaining,” Lagradante said.
(His license is currently administratively revoked. Under our rules, he must surrender [the firearms], but the latest information is that the remaining firearms are still being accounted for.)
On May 27, the PNP revoked the firearms licenses of dela Rosa, who is facing an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC).
PNP revokes Bato dela Rosa’s 117 firearms licenses
The order was issued by the FEO, citing a pending criminal case carrying a penalty of more than two years as grounds for recommending the revocation of dela Rosa’s gun licenses.

The ICC issued an arrest warrant for dela Rosa in connection with the crimes against humanity case involving former President Rodrigo Duterte over alleged extrajudicial killings during the war on drugs.— MCG, GMA News

articles.summary: Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. on Monday defended the police response to a teachers' rally held around the Malacañang Complex.

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 2:47pm
Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. on Monday defended the police response to a teachers' rally held around the Malacañang Complex.
At a press briefing, Nartatez said the police officers were only enforcing rules on public assemblies and ensuring the safety of protesters and other people in the area.
“Meron tayong rally zone unang-una and that is not Malacañang area in front of simbahan,” he said.
(First, we have a rally zone, and that is not Malacanang area in front of church.)

“Supposed to be hindi naman sila dapat gagawa, doon dapat sila sa freedom park, freedom zone at doon sila maglabas maski maghapon pa at siyempre nandiyan pa rin ang pulis for them ay maging safe sila doon sa activity nila,” he added.

(They are supposed to be not doing anything, they should be in freedom park, freedom zone and they can go out there even for the entire day and of course the police are still there for them to be safe during their activities.)
Nartatez said protesters are expected to hold their activities in designated freedom parks or rally zones, citing Batas Pambansa Bilang 880, or the Public Assembly Act of 1985.
He said holding an assembly outside designated areas may constitute an illegal assembly, prompting police to ask protesters to peacefully disperse.
Nartatez stressed that the police were not trying to curtail the teachers' right to protest.
“We are asking them to peacefully disperse,” he said.
Nartatez said that the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) is now studying ways to prevent similar incidents and ensure that dispersals are handled properly.
On Sunday, tensions flared during the protest as scuffles broke out between participating teachers and government security personnel.
Security personnel from the Presidential Security Command were seen blocking and pushing back rallyists who attempted to stage a demonstration in front of a school inside the Malacañang Complex.
ACT Philippines strongly condemned what it described as the violent dispersal of protesters by police outside Malacañang.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Australia experiences second hottest September on record as El Niño and climate crisis combine
articles.summary:
Alpine areas also experience record-breaking heat with snow depth recorded at zero in Kosciuszko national park

Australia had its second hottest September on record last month as global…

blocks.text: Australia had its second hottest September on record last month as global heating and a strengthening El Niño combined to break a string of heat records around the country.

Bureau of Meteorology data showed the minimum night-time temperatures across the continent were also the hottest for any September on a record that goes back to 1910. Averaged temperatures ranked in the top five warmest Septembers for every state, and the sixth hottest for the Northern Territory.
Alpine areas also broke temperature records, and in Kosciuszko national park snow depth fell to zero in September for the first time since monitoring started in 1954.
“There’s only one clear driver of this and that’s climate change,” said Dr Linden Ashcroft, a climate scientist at the University of Melbourne.
“This is also a clear example of seasonal creep where winter is ending earlier and spring is starting sooner.”

blocks.caption: A map showing temperatures across Australia for September 2026. Illustration: Bureau of Meteorology

blocks.text: Across the continent, average temperatures for September were 2.71C above the long-term 1961 to 1990 average. Minimum temperatures were 2.52C above average for the month, just beating the previous mark of 2.51C set in 2023.
The bureau’s data showed Australia has not experienced a September with below average mean temperatures since 2004.
Global heating has warmed the continent by more than 1.5C since country-wide records began in 1910.

All states and territories had below average rainfall for September except for Western Australia, which had its second wettest September on record and the wettest September since 1904. In NSW, 45 locations recorded their warmest Septembers on record.
Dr Simon Grainger, a senior climatologist at the bureau, said: “It was pretty much just warm everywhere.

“There were persistent high-pressure systems over south-east Australia, and that kept the days quite warm and meant the days were quite dry. It was the fourth driest September on record for New South Wales and the sixth driest for Victoria.
“It’s unusual to see this persistent lack of cold days.”

Alongside global warming, Grainger said the El Niño climate system that is still intensifying in the tropical Pacific – forecast to be the strongest ever recorded – had likely contributed to the heat and rainfall patterns seen in September.
Several alpine weather stations – where many ski resorts closed early after a warm and rainy winter – also set records in September.

The bureau said data from Snowy Hydro’s monitoring gauge at Spencers Creek in Kosciuszko National Park showed snow depth had fallen to zero during September – the first time this had happened in any September since records started in 1954.
At Thredbo, where temperatures measurements go back 59 years, the average night-time temperature was 0.1C – the first time the daily minimum for September had averaged above freezing.
The town also saw its hottest September day on record at 16C, some 1C over the previous record set in 2001.
In Victoria’s alpine regions, maximum temperatures across the month in Mount Buller, Falls Creek and Mount Hotham were all the hottest on record.

articles.title: Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
articles.summary: Yemen's internationally recognized government announced a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory after rebels cut a key road linking the city of Taiz with Aden.

image.caption: The recent Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the besieged city of Taiz [September 22, 2014]Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yemen's Saudi-backed government on Sunday announced a new military operation to retake territory held by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, as fighting intensified around the key southwestern city of Taiz.

"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni Presidential Council chief Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
The announcement came after Houthi fighters captured a key road linking Taiz with the government-held city of Aden, effectively isolating Taiz. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.
More than 70 people were reportedly killed in fighting around Taiz over the past day, according to AFP news agency.

blocks.caption: The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire [FILE: September 27, 2026]Image: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: How did the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthis escalate?

The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia, reviving Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.
As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Last month, the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands, even as Al-Alimi called for support from the international community.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.

Former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco’s camp on Monday said they will answer all the allegations against him once they have reviewed the documents, adding that they only formally received the affidavit of former police patrolman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. today.

Lawyer Rowell Ilagan appeared before the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to answer its invite following Gracioso’s allegations that he delivered cash to Vice President Sara Duterte, Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte, and former president Rodrigo Duterte on Velasco’s instructions.
“Sasagutin po namin sa tamang panahon. We will address all the allegations. So pakihintay na lang po,” Ilagan said in an ambush interview.
(We will answer at the proper time. We will address all the allegations. So please just wait.)
“Lahat po ng allegation sa affidavit niya, sasagutin po namin,” he added.
(All the allegations in his affidavit, we will answer.)
Ilagan said that they are also willing and ready to participate at any time.
Meanwhile, when asked to confirm if the houses raided by NBI agents in August belonged to Velasco, the lawyer reiterated that they will answer at the right time.
“Ngayon lang po namin na-receive formally ‘yung affidavit ni Gracioso so hindi po kami puwedeng mag-issue ng ano mang statement hangga’t hindi official copy ng mga documents,” he said.
(We only formally received Gracioso’s affidavit just now, so we cannot issue any statement until we have the official copy of the documents.)

“Sa panahon po ngayon, ang dali mameke, mag fabricate ng mga ebidensya. Kaya sinasabi namin na maging mapanuri po tayo sa lahat ng alegasyon at sa lahat ng ebidensya na pinapakita sa social media kasi dapat i-test po natin ito,” he added.

(Nowadays, it is so easy to fake things and fabricate evidence. That is why we are saying that we should be critical of all allegations and all evidence presented on social media because we have to test them.)
Velasco’s camp previously said the allegations against him had “no basis.”
The Philippine National Police (PNP) earlier confirmed that Gracioso had been previously suspended and demoted prior to his dismissal from the service this month.
PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. also said that Gracioso had previously been assigned to the security detail of Velasco who was then House speaker.

articles.title: PNP: Focus crimes dropped by 29.75% in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said it has recorded a 29.75% decline in focus crimes over the 3rd quarter - July to September 2026 - compared to the same period in 2025 Focus crimes…

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 2:06pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said it has recorded a 29.75% decline in focus crimes over the 3rd quarter – July to September 2026 – compared to the same period in 2025

Focus crimes are offenses considered serious in nature and occur with sufficient frequency and regularity. These include murder, homicide, physical injury, rape, robbery, theft, carnapping of motor vehicles, and carnapping of motorcycles.
At a press briefing, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said data showed that 7,233 cases were recorded during the three months, down from 10,296 cases in the same period in 2025.
“The overall crime situation continues to improve. With eight focus crimes, posting a clear decline in 2026 compared with the last year,” he said.
“From July to September this year, we recorded 7,233 cases, a decrease of 3,000 cases from the 10,296 recorded during the same period last year. It is 29.75% lower,” he added.
In September alone, focus crime cases fell by 36% to 2,063 from 3,226 a year earlier.
The PNP said the decline showed its sustained police operations and other crime prevention programs.
Also, the PNP reported intensified operations against organized criminal groups and repeat offenders.
In September, the PNP conducted 3,140 anti-smuggling operations, resulting in 564 arrests and the confiscation of smuggled goods and other items estimated at P1.36 billion.
The PNP also reported 8,447 arrests of wanted persons during the month, including 2,254 most wanted individuals.
Authorities likewise continued their campaign against loose firearms, which the PNP identified as one of the factors contributing to crimes such as murder, homicide, physical injuries, and robbery.
During the period, 979 people were arrested, while 6,381 firearms were accounted for and another 913 were turned over for safekeeping. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Alleged flydubai attacker left Australia without finishing engineering course, university says
articles.summary:
RMIT confirms co-pilot was a student as Australian authorities examine his time in country between 2015 and 2017

An Australian university has confirmed a flydubai co-pilot who allegedly…

blocks.text: An Australian university has confirmed a flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound flight studied at its Melbourne campus, but left before completing his qualification.

Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, identified by media outlets as Hammam al-Hammami, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.

The United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said the co-pilot allegedly used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air. Numerous media outlets have named the co-pilot al-Hammami, an Omani national.
On Monday, the RMIT university in Melbourne said in a statement that it “is aware of media reporting of a former student alleged to be involved in the Flydubai flight incident”.
“The individual was enrolled at RMIT but did not successfully complete an engineering qualification,” the university
“As this is an ongoing investigation, the University is unable to provide further comment.”
Former RMIT engineering students contacted by Guardian Australia said they did not remember al-Hammami.
RMIT university’s confirmation came after the Australian federal police (AFP) on Sunday said agencies were investigating the man’s time in the country.

A source familiar with the case, but not authorised to speak publicly, has said the man was granted an Australian student visa in 2014, before arriving in the country to commence a university course the next year.
He left Australia in 2017, and his visa was cancelled in 2019 after authorities confirmed he was no longer enrolled in the course, the source said.
The AFP on Sunday said multiple agencies – including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (Asio) – were probing the man’s connections to the country.
“The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man’s links to Australia,” an AFP spokesperson said.
“An update will be provided at an appropriate time.”

Court records and previous media reporting show that a number of Australians charged with terror offences or suspected of Islamic extremism studied at RMIT around the same time as al-Hammami, but there was no indication he knew any of these individuals.

A British university, Buckinghamshire New University, has confirmed a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management”. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.”
A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still ‌under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further.

The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv were suspended after the attack. The Omani co-pilot and the flight’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.

articles.summary: The Supreme Court will hear pleas against India's beleagured poll body chief over alleged unilateral decisions related to the large-scale revision of voter lists. DW has the latest.

image.caption: The hearing comes after thousands of protesters and opposition supporters rallied in Delhi and Mumbai over the weekend to demand Kumar's resignationImage: Abiraj Kumar Arulgnanakumar/DW

blocks.text: The Supreme Court will hear pleas against India's beleagured poll body chief over alleged unilateral decisions related to the large-scale revision of voter lists. DW has the latest.

blocks.caption: The hearing comes after thousands of protesters and opposition supporters rallied in Delhi and Mumbai over the weekend to demand Kumar's resignationImage: Abiraj Kumar Arulgnanakumar/DW

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: India's Supreme Court will hear petitions against the functioning of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid voter list controversy
Meanwhile, protests are seeking Kumar's resignation

blocks.text: Here are the latest developments from India on Monday, October 5.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
October 5, 2026
Supreme Court to hear petitions against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR decisions

The Supreme Court on Monday is scheduled to hear a batch of pleas seeking the suspension of Election Commission of India chief Gyanesh Kumar over decisions related to the country's controversial voter roll revisions, allegedly taken unilaterally, India media reported.

Critics say a nationwide voter-verification exercise — called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — which began last year, has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters by striking their names from electoral rolls

Kumar has been under intense public scrutiny after the Indian Express daily reported that two of his fellow election commissioners raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral roll data, but those concerns were not taken into consideration.
Kumar heads the three-member commission, which has overseen the voter roll revisions.

The Election Commission of India rejects allegations of wrongdoing and says the process removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Opposition parties and critics allege that the changes to voter lists benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge the party denies.
Kumar is yet to make a comment on the allegations against him.

On Monday, a three-judge bench, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, is expected to hear petitions over the decisions taken by Kumar allegedly without the approval of the two election commissioners.

One of the petitions is seeking a declaration that the chief election commissioner cannot take decisions for the ECI without the concurrence of the other two Election Commissioners, legal news website LiveLaw reported.

The other seeks a revocation of the 14 reported decisions allegedly taken unilaterally, along with the constitution of an independent judicial inquiry commission or a special investigation team headed by a retired judge of the Supreme Court to probe the allegations against Kumar.
The hearing comes afterthousands of protesters and opposition supporters rallied in Delhi and Mumbai over the weekend to demand Kumar's resignation.

articles.title: Hundreds of French schools closed amid protests
articles.summary: The student protests that rocked France last week have prompted authorities to keep up to 500 schools closed on Monday. More protests are planned for Tuesday.

image.caption: The school protests have spread nationwide, as here in LyonImage: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Several hundred schools in France will close totally or partially on Monday amid security fears following a wave of nationwide student protests, the education minister has said.
The protests by pupils complaining of poor conditions began at one Paris school on September 17 but last week mutated into sometimes violent demonstrations across the nation.
France students protest school conditions
Why are the schools staying closed?
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be totally or partly suspended" in some "400-500" high schools on Monday, as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled."
According to Geffray, the schools were being closed mainly as a precaution, with more large protests planned for Tuesday.
Geffray said the number of schools remaining closed on Monday would be similar to that on Friday but that there was planned to be a "partial, progressive return to lessons."
He said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff members injured since the protests began.

"There are activists — particularly from the far left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Geffray said.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he added.
Valerie Pecresse, the president of the Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital, said that more than a third of the 468 schools in the region would be shut on Monday.

blocks.caption: Several schools have been damaged amid the protestsImage: CLPRESS/ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: What are the school protesters saying?
The protesting teenagers at French high schools, called lycees, have complained of high rates of absenteeism by teachers, school days that are too long and dilapidated facilities.

They have also protested at the lack of adequate cooling on hot summer days, with some towns seeing temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenehit) last summer in a country without widespread air conditioning.
Organizers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government was still failing to proposed "concrete measures" to remedy the situation.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu urged local authorities to make it a priority to fill gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts.
He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss renovating school buildings that are often in poor condition.
Violent incidents at the school protests
The protests have been marked by several violent incidents, with security forces sometimes using tear gas and batons to disperse the young protesters.
More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement.
On Sunday, a 16-year-old was detained after a 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a protest in the southern town of La Ciotat.
Last week, a group of young people was filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in the eastern town of Belfort.
The French branch of rights group Amnesty International last week described the action taken by police as "disproportionate."

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has, however, defended security forces, saying they were "not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands."

articles.title: Monday briefing: You asked, we answered – how will the US midterms go?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: As Americans get ready to vote on whether the Republican party remains in control of Congress, our Washington editor talks about the disconnect between Trump and his…

blocks.text: Good morning. Later today, Donald Trump will be in the state of Nebraska to rev up supporters as he kicks off a campaign blitz of rallies ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November.

If his early speeches are anything to go by, cornhuskers can anticipate poll denial, accusations of veganism and an expletive ratio that my nine-year-old would love. And Nebraskans may love it, too: aside from one “blue dot” district in Omaha, Republicans argue their support is steady in the state that has easily backed Trump three times.

This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote, and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base.

I asked First Edition readers what you really want to know about the US midterms. Today, in a happy exercise in newsletter cross-pollination, I put your questions to our Washington editor Ankita Rao, who runs our US elections newsletter The Stakes. First, the headlines.
Weekend roundup

items: UK politics | The Greens in England and Wales have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.

Schools | Lawyers and campaigners have condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s are reported to police each year.

Brazil | Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.

Environment | A study of Europe’s summer paints a grim picture for the future, with doctors and climate scientists calling on governments to stop burning fossil fuels, shade buildings, green cities, and install air conditioning in hospitals, schools and care homes.
US military | The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘We are prepared for anything’

blocks.caption: Donald Trump at a campaign rally in Omaha, Nebraska in 2020. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

blocks.text: You’d be forgiven, readers, if the state of US politics is perplexing you. On the one hand, there are voters who have little faith in the president’s war in the Middle East and are increasingly angry about his inability to make daily life more affordable at home.
On the other, Trump has promised a “big surprise” come 3 November – and polls have predicted the wrong results for previous elections.
As Ankita Rao set out in The Stakes in September, her team of reporters across the US are hearing the same things in almost every community they’ve spent time in:

Americans feel their lives are dictated by an elite class that goes beyond political parties – best summed up by Democratic senator Jon Ossoff’s use of the term “Epstein class”. People are exhausted by an ongoing crisis in affordability of childcare, healthcare, food and gas. Many have lost trust in institutions, from hospitals to schools.
With this deep knowledge of the mood of the country, she is the woman to answer your questions. Over to you.
Who still believes in Donald Trump? Johanne, Quebec, Canada

Ankita’s short answer is that it might be the other way around: a lot of Americans don’t feel they’ve been presented with a better option yet. This was evident during primary season, when both Democrats and Republicans went for candidates “who they felt would actually stick it to the man”, says Ankita, rather than regurgitating established party platforms.

After all, that was what so many hoped to get with Trump – but those voters who had flocked to him as the anti-establishment leader, or the man who represented something beyond the two-party system, now see him aligning himself with big tech and other corporate interests, particularly this last term in office.

There’s a serious disconnect between Trump and his supporters, Ankita tells me. His previously impressive political instincts have faltered “partly because he can’t see beyond his own fixations” – be that his ballroom, the war in Iran, or the unfettered growth of AI.
As one Ohio voter told us at the weekend: “I’m sorry, but I don’t give a shit whose name is on the Kennedy Center.”
Has Trump got a decisive ‘dirty trick’ up his sleeve? Bron Purkiss, England

A big concern for First Edition readers is election interference: how Trump has already restricted voting and what dirty tricks he might still try. Will he try to ignore the election results – and how would the Guardian report that?

Ankita joined Guardian US seven years ago as voting rights editor, launching our multiyear democracy project. “We had four reporters on that, but now they’re part of the larger politics team, and election integrity has become essential to our coverage,” she says.

In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump signed executive orders seeking to assert more control over voting methods, and in a Time magazine interview last week, he refused to rule out declaring a national emergency around elections to implement them. “So we are prepared for anything,” says Ankita.

Legal challenges in individual races are “almost inevitable”, she says. “We know the states where the election systems are fully controlled by Republicans, and we’re ready to move everybody there if we see anything strange happening”. Fear of election rigging is high in the communities Guardian reporters are visiting. “We hear this a lot from Democrats who are worried about making sure their vote counts, and more nervous about using mail-in ballots.” This September edition of The Stakes covers Trump’s attempts to restrict postal voting – which is how almost one-third of Americans vote.
Ankita suggests this could result in higher turnout. Early data in the deeply red state of Florida, for example, showed voter registration among Democrats already very high.
“There’s a sense that ‘we need to go out in droves and make sure that all of these wins are very decisive, so that nobody can question them’.”
Would Republican losses limit Trump’s excesses? Peter Alexander, England

Ankita tells me she doesn’t make predictions any more – a lot can change in a few short weeks – but if an election was called tomorrow “it looks as if the Democrats will absolutely win the House and most likely win the Senate”.

The mechanics of voting mean that it will take a decisive majority in both chambers to act as a genuine bulwark against Trump, says Ankita, before adding the weighty caveat that Trump sidestepped congressional authorisation altogether ahead of the Iran war.

Nonetheless, she anticipates a slew of investigations after the midterms, launched in the House and then requiring the Senate to move them forward. For example, there are already calls for an investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of Donald Trump Jr’s recent wedding in the Bahamas.
How will democratic socialists influence policy decisions after the midterms? Feride Hekimgil, Turkey

This is a “huge question”, Ankita agrees, as progressive candidates capture the enthusiasm of voters desperate for radical change. While the number of Democratic Socialists actually elected is likely to only be a handful, it could become a “very vocal group”.

What’s not clear yet is how they will act once in the Congress. Ankita points to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists: “She was very clear about her affiliation when she ran, but she hasn’t been that type of lawmaker where she exists to stop the party from doing certain things. She has been much more strategic and collaborative with establishment Democrats.”

It remains to be seen whether an augmented group after 3 November takes a similar route or choses a more hardline stance, in particular on Israel’s decimation of Gaza, which has already created gaping divisions in the Democratic party.
One more thing

In an early edition of The Stakes, Ankita described her morning bike ride to the Guardian’s Washington office, navigating National Guard trucks and reflecting on the militarisation of her city since the last election. I wanted to ask her, as a citizen as well as a journalist, how that influences the way she approaches this election.
after newsletter promotion

It can’t be overstated, she tells me, how it changes your day-to-day life: “It adds a layer of subtle fear. I’m not actively scared about walking around DC, but it feels as if things could escalate really quickly.”

Will it hold people back from voting, or at least displaying their preferences? Quite the opposite, she tells me. “Places where we see this military presence – in Minneapolis, or LA, or DC – are such vocal, largely Democratic cities that people are undeterred.”
“There are double the number of lawn signs,” she says. “It’s defiant.”
For more from Ankita and the Guardian US politics in the run-up to the midterms, sign up to The Stakes 2026 here
The week to come

items: Tuesday | ABC News is suing the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) over its licence review, and on Thursday its hearing will take place. The broadcaster claims the review, ordered by Donald Trump in April over comedian Jimmy Kimmel’s comments about the US president, is a “retaliatory campaign” in violation of its first amendment rights.

Wednesday | Kemi Badenoch is to speak at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. This day also marks the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks by Hamas. In London, the Met are asking organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march to move the event.
Thursday | Holborn and St Pancras will hold its byelection. The seat belongs to former prime minister and Labour party leader Keir Starmer, who held it from 2015 until his resignation in September.

blocks.text: What else we’ve been enjoying

blocks.caption: Grin and bear it … a photo by Charles Janson. Photograph: Comedy wildlife awards 2026

items: Helena Horton’s sweeping interview with the Royal Horticultural Society boss Clare Matterson is an absorbing conversation about everything from her high hopes for Andy Burnham, the roles of gardens in public health and the RHS’s £2.3m roadworks compensation. “Who is gardening for in the 21st century?” Matterson asks. “Is it for a small elite band of people, or is it for everybody?” Craille Maguire Gillies, newsletters team

If you didn’t catch it yesterday, our interview with the actor John Boyega, recounting the impact of seeing his close friend Damilola Taylor die when he was a child, is deeply moving. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

blocks.text: Sport

blocks.caption: Manchester City’s Bunny Shaw scores the fourth goal to seal victory over Arsenal and top spot in the WSL. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

blocks.text: Football | Manchester City came from behind on two occasions to beat Arsenal 4-2 ⁠in the Women’s Super League on Sunday, keeping the champions top of the table.

Racing | Formula One drivers have issued a damning condemnation of the sport’s engine regulations that caused the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to open with scenes of cars stopping on track and unable to accelerate because of software problems. Max Verstappen got his first win of the season at the chaotic race.
Football | The Republic of Ireland’s manager Heimir Hallgrímsson has called on Uefa to keep his side away from Israel in future draws after a pair of fixtures he admitted “has been tough on us all”.
The front pages

blocks.caption: Photograph: Guardian

blocks.text: The Guardian leads with “Horryfying scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools revealed”. The Times splashes with “Badenoch to pledge a bonfire of green laws” and the Mail has “Kemi’s common sense blueprint”. The Mirror, on Badenoch’s pledges to cut benefits, goes with “Bad to the future”. The Telegraph has “Andrew takes police to court over arrest” and The Financial Times says “Hopes for record year in dealmaking punctured by interest rate increases”. The i Paper runs with “Man City owners’ link to Burnham’s No 10 North site after ‘sweetheart deal’ with UAE firm”. And the Sun leads with a story on the romance between Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates, headlined “Love match of the day”.

Features writer Elle Hunt and Indigenous activist María José Andrade Cerda on the growing phenomenon of influencers around the world trying to reach uncontacted tribes.

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Barbara Scully performing at the Funny Women comedy show at Whelans, Dublin. Photograph: Paul Sherwood

blocks.text: Five years ago, Barbara Scully sat in her car crying. Trying to find work after taking time to raise her children, she found herself facing closed doors. “I presume it was the fact that I was 50 and had a 10-year gap where my career used to live [while she was raising children],” she says. “I sat in the car on the driveway in tears, thinking: that’s it, I’m washed up, I’m done.”
Then something changed. “Once I pulled myself together, I thought: OK, if this were one of my kids, what would I tell them? … Look at what it is you enjoy doing and try to make that work for you.”

Scully relaunched her career for the sixth time, as a broadcaster and comedian, and feels happier than ever. “I am on a mission to try to tell women in particular not to fear getting older; to embrace it, to push back against all the bullshit about how you should be fighting ageing,” she says.

articles.title: California woman arrested and accused of spying on Taiwan president’s son for China
articles.summary:
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport before she left for China, the agency said

US authorities arrested a California ⁠woman on…

blocks.text: US authorities arrested a California ⁠woman on ​Sunday, accusing her of spying on the son of Taiwan’s president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.

The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the agency said in a ⁠statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.

Zhang surveilled a ​son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the ‌FBI alleged. The agency ‌did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report ‌identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident.
Taiwan’s presidential office described Zhang’s alleged actions as a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.
“Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
China’s foreign ministry did not respond to ‌a request for comment.

The Justice Department alleged Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and licence plate information of the Taiwanese president’s son and his family.

Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection ⁠and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, ​the first assistant US ​attorney for the Central District of ​California, alleged in a statement.
It was not immediately clear whether Zhang ​had a defence attorney. She ‌will appear on ​Monday in a ​Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said.

Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as ​Chinese territory. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.
Washington does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is the island’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.

articles.title: DA: Fuel subsidies for farmers, fisherfolk to start soon amid El Niño threat
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) said Monday that fuel subsidies for farmers and fisherfolk amid the threat of a potentially very strong El Niño will begin soon, with registered fisherfolk set to…

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 1:35pm

The Department of Agriculture (DA) said Monday that fuel subsidies for farmers and fisherfolk amid the threat of a potentially very strong El Niño will begin soon, with registered fisherfolk set to receive assistance this week.
For mechanized farmers, the department said it is eyeing to start releasing the fuel subsidy by the last week of October or in November.
“For fisherfolk, distribution will start this week. As for farmers, they (DA personnel) are cleaning up the list," Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said in a press briefing.
"The latest would be the first week of November, but hopefully before the end of October, the assistance for our farmers will be released as well," he added.
The fuel assistance is part of the P6.2 billion released by the Department of Budget and Management through the Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) program.
The DA said it will prioritize the release of fuel subsidies to farmers and fisherfolk in areas affected by the Habagat and those that experienced drought in the past, mostly in Luzon.

“For priority areas, we are prioritizing Habagat-affected areas, basically Zambales, Tarlac, Pampanga and Bulacan. And of course, those hit by drought in Isabela and those that experienced extreme heat in the past,” said Tiu Laurel.

State weather bureau PAGASA said the upcoming El Niño could last until March or even June. Around 40 provinces are expected to experience below-normal rainfall during the dry spell and drought, while the number of affected provinces could double by January.
Aside from drier weather, temperatures are also expected to rise, with some areas experiencing temperatures as high as 38.7 degrees Celsius.
Tiu Laurel said the DA requested a total of P45 billion to fund its mitigation measures for El Niño. This includes the initial P6.2 billion allocation for fuel subsidies under the UPLIFT program.

“The total amount we requested is P45 billion. Actually, later this afternoon, we have a meeting in Malacañang with the President specifically about El Niño. We meet almost weekly. The P6.2 billion is just the initial amount,” said Tiu Laurel.
The DA earlier said it would adopt a “scientific” strategy to mitigate the impact of a potentially record-breaking El Niño.

The DA also assured that it is preparing a bigger food buffer to cushion the impact of the possible extreme drought by expanding rice storage capacity and opening more cold storage facilities.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Middle East oil exports recover to pre-Iran war levels despite Hormuz attacks
articles.summary: Gulf crude exports returned to pre-war levels in September, with producers increasingly relying on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers to bypass Hormuz. Iranian exports remain below the…

image.caption: Before the Iran war started, the Strait of Hormuz accounted for some 20% of the world’s daily crude oil and LNG supply [FILE: July 21, 2019]Image: Morteza Akhoundi/ISNA/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: Middle East crude oil exports, excluding Iran, rose back above pre-war levels in late September despite continued attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, according shipping data from trade intelligence firm Kpler.

Exports exceeded the pre-war average of about 18 million barrels per day (bpd) on four days in the final week of September, reaching 19.5 million to 22.5 million bpd, according to the data and analytics platform.
When the Strait of Hormuz closed following the start of the Iran war, the seven-day average non-Iranian crude leaving the region fell by 72% in 10 days, Kpler said.
How was Hormuz bypassed?
The recovery has relied on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers.
In September, about 40% of crude left the Gulf without crossing Hormuz, compared with only 17% before the Iran war.
According to Kpler, more than 70% of the crude changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman in August. In comparison, almost no Gulf crude changed tankers in the Gulf of Oman before the war.
Additionally, Saudi Arabia also increased exports through the Red Sea, while the UAE used its pipeline to Fujairah.
The primary exporters of crude oil in the region were:

items: Saudi Arabia
the United Arab Emirates
Iraq

blocks.text: Iran, however, remains the major exception, with its exports still well below the pre-war average, primarily due to US policies.
Attacks on ships around Hormuz continue
Meanwhile, attacks on vessels have continued around Hormuz. At least seven incidents have been reported in recent weeks.
On October 1, a tanker, Kazimah III, was reportedly struck by an unknown projectile, according to maritime intelligence firm Marisks. All crew members were evacuated safely.

articles.title: Truck operators to suspend trips Oct. 6, citing issues 'worse' than during pandemic
articles.summary: The group says shipping delays, truck bans and a driver shortage are also hurting operations.

blocks.text: Cargo trucks queue along Road 10 at the North Harbor Port in Manila on September 15, 2022.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — A group of truck operators will temporarily suspend trips for three days starting Tuesday, October 6, in what it calls a transport holiday to press the government to address problems in the trucking industry.
The Confederation of Truckers Association of the Philippines said Monday, October 5, that high fuel costs and problems involving shipping line operations are among its biggest concerns.

"Halimbawa babyahe kami ngayong Lunes, hindi na namin alam kung kailan ang susunod na byahe dahil 'yung empty containers namin, walang sapat na espasyo ang shipping lines para isauli at paglagyan, para mabakante kami at makabyahe kami ulit," CTAP President Mary Zapata said in an interview with dzMM.

(For example, if we make a trip this Monday, we don't know when our next trip will be because shipping lines don't have enough space for us to return and store our empty containers. Until we can return them and free up our trucks, we cannot make another trip.)
The truckers group also raised concerns over unregulated destination charges, truck ban policies that disrupt operations and a shortage of truck drivers.

"Walang kita, talagang napakalaki na ng problema namin. Sinasabi nga namin, ako in my personal assessment, itong sitwasyon ng trucking industry by this time is even worse nung pandemic time," Zapata said.
(We're not making any money, and the problem has become very serious. In my personal assessment, the trucking industry is in an even worse situation now than it was during the pandemic.)
Impact on goods, economy
Zapata said problems in the industry can affect the wider economy because trucks move goods from manufacturing plants and warehouses to retailers and consumers.
She said a three-day suspension of trips could have a significant economic impact. But even without the transport holiday, she said trucking operations are already limited, hurting operators' income.
The group is seeking a direct dialogue with the government and concrete solutions to its concerns.

"Makita naman nila 'yung important role ng truckers sa ating ekonomiya... Alam na alam naman halos ito ng lahat ng government offices na concerned sa transpo. Nasabihan na namin ito but then wala eh. Pinakikinggan naman kami, ine-entertain kami, but as of now, wala pa kaming makitang solusyon," Zapata said.

(I hope they see the important role truckers play in our economy... Almost all government offices concerned with transportation are already aware of these issues. We have raised them, and while they listen to us, we still have not seen any solution.)

articles.title: Tongol: Dec. 16 a 'logistical projection,' not a deadline for impeachment court
articles.summary: Impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol said Monday that the December 16 schedule he mentioned earlier should not be seen as a deadline for the impeachment court to issue a verdict on the…

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 1:16pm

Impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol said Monday that the December 16 schedule he mentioned earlier should not be seen as a deadline for the impeachment court to issue a verdict on the case of Vice President Sara Duterte.
In an interview ahead of Day 33 of the impeachment trial, Tongol clarified that the date was only based on administrative plotting or logistical projection hinged on the pre-trial order calendar.

“Pero I agree, and I appreciate the correction and clarification of the senator-judges of that target date dahil hindi po ito dapat na tignan na bilang deadline para sa ating impeachment court. Dahil ang kanilang concern po ay ‘yung integrity ng impeachment proceeding na dapat ay mabigyan ng pagkakataon ang lahat na mailatag ang kanilang ebidensya,” the court spokesperson explained.

(But I agree with, and appreciate, the correction and clarification made by the senator-judges regarding that target date, because it should not be viewed as a deadline for our impeachment court. Their concern is the integrity of the impeachment proceedings and ensuring that everyone is given the opportunity to present their evidence.)
“Ang kanilang sinasabi lamang sa atin na ang ebidensya ay hindi susunod doon sa kalendaryo. Ang kalendaryo ang susunod sa ebidensya,” he added.
(What they are telling us is simply that the evidence must not follow the calendar; the calendar must follow the evidence.)
During the trial, Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo asked the Senate impeachment court to admonish Tongol for telling the media that the verdict in Duterte’s impeachment trial would be out by December 16.
Senator-judge Kiko Pangilinan also earlier thumbed down remarks made by the impeachment court spokesperson, saying that they have had no talks of such a timeline.
For his part, Tongol clarified that the trial may be prolonged or cut short based on the evidence presented.

“Kung makita ng impeachment court na kailangan nang mas mahabang paglatag ng mga ebidensya, then mauurong pa ‘yun, ‘yung date na ‘yun. At kung ito naman ay nakita na maraming stipulations na nagawa at maraming dropping of witnesses at dropping of possible articles of impeachment, ito namang date na ‘to ay uurong nang mas maaga pa,” he explained.

(If the impeachment court determines that a more extensive presentation of evidence is needed, then that date will be moved to a later time. On the other hand, if many stipulations are made, and there will be dropping of witnesses and potential articles of impeachment, then the date could be moved up to an earlier time.)
Nevertheless, Tongol said he welcomes the guidance of the senator-judges. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Chiz junks defense bid to block AMLC chief's testimony at Sara trial
articles.summary: Senate court rejects Sara Duterte defense bid to block testimony on financial records.

blocks.text: Impeachment trial presiding officer Chiz Escudero, a senator-judge, as seen during the Senate court proceedings on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026.
Senate PRIB; The STAR screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero allowed the chief of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) to testify on financial transactions involving Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio.

This was after the defense panel, through lawyer Mark Vinluan, had moved to exclude AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura as a witness, arguing that confidentiality rules under the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA) also apply to impeachment proceedings.

"Walang tinatago ang Bise Presidente, ngunit ang mga datos ay dapat dumaan sa tamang proseso ng pagberipika nang naaayon sa batas at hindi dapat ibalandra ang mga ito sa publiko sa pamamaraang mali, malisyoso at ang tanging layon ay pamumulitika lamang," Vinluan said at the proceedings on Monday, October 5.

(The vice president is hiding nothing, but the data must go through the proper verification process in accordance with the law and should not be paraded before the public in a manner that is improper, malicious and solely intended for political mudslinging.)
In rejecting the motion, Escudero said AMLA's confidentiality rules must be observed but do not make AMLC reports immune from compulsory processes.
"Compliance with a lawful order subject to proper safeguards does not constitute, to the mind of the court, such a breach," Escudero said.

The confidentiality provision is intended to prevent leaks and unauthorized disclosure of AMLC information, rather than prevent the council from carrying out its investigative and litigation functions, Escudero said.
He said the AMLC is not just a repository of information and must still be allowed to perform its duties.
Unexplained wealth arguments
The impeachment court is taking up Article II on Monday, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth and financial discrepancies involving the vice president.
Prosecution lawyer Mae Divinagracia said Buenaventura would testify that "billions worth of transactions passed through the accounts" of Duterte and Carpio.
In the prosecution's offer of testimony, Divinagracia said at least "P1.6 billion came in, at least P1.3 billion went out, and no record shows where it went."
The prosecution also alleged that Carpio "walked out of two banks with P41 million in cash in a single day."
It further claimed that money from China flowed into a food company linked to Carpio, where Duterte was named as an incorporator.
The prosecution's offer also includes a claim that a person allegedly linked to illegal drugs purchased checks worth about P14.88 million naming Duterte as beneficiary in 2011 and 2012.
The allegations form part of the prosecution's presentation under Article II and have yet to be ruled upon by the impeachment court.

articles.title: Authorities issue shark warning over whale that swam 11km upstream in Clarence River and later died
articles.summary:
The juvenile humpback was spotted near Bundjalung National Park in what experts say is a rare, but not unprecedented event

While the case of a whale found 11km upstream in a New South Wales…

blocks.text: While the case of a whale found 11km upstream in a New South Wales river this weekend was unusual, it was not unprecedented, experts say.
The juvenile humpback, which swam into the Clarence River on the state’s mid-north coast and later died, was towed out to sea on Sunday, according to NSW authorities.

Members of the public first reported a sick whale swimming into the river near Bundjalung national park on Saturday afternoon. “The whale subsequently swam onto a sandbar and became grounded in shallow water, and within 30 minutes observers indicated the whale had died,” a spokesperson for NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service said.

Increased shark activity in the surrounding area had been reported, with beachgoers advised to avoid surfing, swimming, or diving at surrounding beaches, SharkSmart NSW said in a post to social media.

Whale scientist Dr Vanessa Pirotta said while the circumstances were rare, whales were known to explore rivers and estuaries from “time to time”. This could be the result of “misadventure” or “curiosity”, or due to ill health, as appeared likely for the animal in Clarence River, which looked “extremely unwell”.

Most whales wouldn’t be aiming for the river at this time of year, she said. “Right now the main bulk of the east and the west coast populations are heading south to Antarctica. They’re on their way back for their summertime extended Christmas dinner where they’ll be going to Antarctica to feed on krill.”
Earlier this year, in April, another whale became stranded on a sandbar in Wallis Lake on the NSW coast after swimming under the Forster Tuncurry Bridge.
Last year, two humpbacks swam under Melbourne’s West Gate Bridge and into the mouth of the Yarra River.
In 2020, three humpback whales entered the East Alligator River in Kakadu national park, with one travelling 30km upstream. All three eventually made their way back out to sea.

While these air-breathing mammals could survive in fresh water environments, it probably wasn’t good for their skin, Pirotta said. Anyone spotting a whale in an unusual location such as a river, or an animal that appeared to be in distress should alert environmental authorities, she said.

A spokesperson for Orrca, the cetacean rescue organisation, said while it was unusual for a whale to travel several kilometres into a river system, it was not unprecedented. “Humpback whales regularly travel close to the NSW coastline and may enter bays, harbours and estuarine environments temporarily during their annual migration.”

Based on the large number of barnacles and other organisms on its skin, the juvenile in the Clarence River could have been experiencing a chronic illness, injury or another underlying health issue, the spokesperson said. “However, the cause of death cannot be determined from imagery alone,” they noted.

“Each year, approximately 50,000 humpback whales migrate along Australia’s east coast. Across a population of this size, it is unfortunately not uncommon for a small proportion of animals to be observed in poor body condition or displaying other signs of illness, injury or compromised health.”
The unusual event occurred less than a week after a humpback whale carcass washed ashore at Perth city beach, and was attracting multiple sharks, before the body was removed on Thursday.

“As with any deceased marine animal, people should avoid entering the water close to the location of the whale carcass, including surrounding beaches, and follow any local warnings or closures that may be in place. Whale carcasses can attract scavengers, including sharks,” the Orrca spokesperson said.
