articles.title: US air force removes all bombers from British military base RAF Fairford
articles.summary: A statement says all bombers deployed to RAF Fairford have been "re-deployed to their home stations" in the US.

blocks.text: The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the UK military base at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter terror police.
A statement from a US department official confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
The US did not give a reason for the withdrawal, but it follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences near the base and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Whitehall sources have not disputed the decision from Washington was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.
The UK's Ministry of Defence has not commented.
Tracking websites showed B-1 bombers flying out of RAF Fairford on Sunday.

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

Initially, five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF). All five were UK nationals from London.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
The sixth man, aged 25, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Counter terror police confirmed on Saturday he had also been released on bail.
RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Days after the incident, and before the arrest of the sixth man, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor".
Rubio did not provide further details - saying at the time he was limited on what he could say on air.
US President Donald Trump separately said he was "surprised" the five men had been released on bail.
"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.
Many B-1 bombers flown from the UK were armed with precision-guided "bunker busting" bombs, with thicker casings to penetrate hardened or buried targets such as weapons stores.
They also carried air-to-surface missiles used against more heavily defended targets deeper inside Iran.
Each bombing mission, depending on the location of the target, would likely have taken around 12 to 15 hours in total there and back, with air-to-air refuelling both ways.
The Pentagon has stressed its bombing aircraft remain able to conduct missions "anywhere, anytime", including through "operations that launch and recover from the continental United States".
Additional reporting by Chris Partridge.

articles.title: Bacolod’s P300M TIEZA projects face scrutiny over delays, defects at cultural landmarks
articles.summary: The controversial TIEZA projects – a P220-million fountain rehabilitation and P80-million public plaza redevelopment – were supposed to be completed last August, ahead of MassKara Festival

items: A P300-million tourism project in Bacolod, intended to enhance public spaces for the MassKara Festival, remains unfinished, leading to criticism from city officials.
Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya expressed dissatisfaction with the project's quality, citing numerous defects and safety hazards, and has refused to sign acceptance documents.

Concerns have been raised about compliance with historical preservation laws, as the Bacolod Public Plaza is a designated national historical landmark, and questions regarding the project's adherence to original proposals have emerged.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BACOLOD, Philippines – A P300-million tourism project package billed as a transformation of two of Bacolod’s most prominent public spaces, one of them a nearly century-old plaza, was supposed to put the city on display for its biggest festival. Instead, it has put the project itself on display, with unfinished work, reported defects and mounting questions over how it was being done.

The Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA) projects – a P220-million rehabilitation of the giant fountain at the Bacolod City Government Center and an P80-million redevelopment of the public plaza – was supposedly completed in August, in time for the MassKara Festival from October 1 to 19.

Instead, both projects remained unfinished as the festival got underway, prompting Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya to publicly criticize the work and say he would not sign acceptance documents unless he was satisfied with the results.

In a letter to TIEZA Chief Operating Officer Mark Lapid, Gasataya said he was “disheartened” by what he saw at the public plaza and listed problems including drainage failures, surface ponding, unsecured fountain nozzles, missing float valves, non-functional lighting, unfinished installations and protruding or deteriorated manholes.

During a visit to the plaza, Gasataya said he observed water pooling around the newly installed centerpiece fountain when it was switched on. He said the fountain’s control sequence had yet to be demonstrated and that the defects he observed constituted safety hazards requiring attention.
Gasataya asked Lapid to intervene and compel the contractor to undertake the necessary corrective work.

He said any redevelopment of the plaza must meet high standards of safety, functionality and aesthetics, describing the site as a central landmark and the traditional heart of Bacolod’s civic gatherings.
The absence of grass in parts of the plaza also irked Gasataya during his inspection.
“Pagsugod n’yo ubra, may hilamon pa ang plaza. Anay manugtapos na kamo, wala na hilamon,” he told project engineers.
(When you started working, the plaza still had grass. Now that you are about to finish, there is no more grass.)
Rappler sought comment from Lapid. Instead, his media officer, Ronnie Calumpita, said they would assess the project first.

The project’s troubled appearance has also drawn criticism from House Deputy Speaker and Bacolod Representative Albee Benitez, the former Bacolod mayor whose administration oversaw the start of the works.
Works that began during the mayorship of Benitez had been expected to be completed by the end of August.
Benitez, who checked the plaza on Wednesday, September 30, said the result was not what had been discussed or proposed.
“Indi amo ni ang aton gin-istoryahan. La-in ang inyo ginpropose. La-in ang outcome,” said Benitez, addressing TIEZA.
(This was not what we talked about. This is not what you proposed. The outcome is different.)

Benitez was referring to the plaza designs that he said had been agreed upon with TIEZA and the contractor. He said any deviation from the original proposal should be explained and addressed with accountability.
There are questions on whether the redevelopment of the Bacolod Public Plaza complied with rules protecting the historic site.

Former Bacolod councilor Ann Marie Palermo, one of the authors of a 2015 city ordinance declaring the plaza a national historical landmark, called on Benitez and others involved in the redevelopment to produce clearance from the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP).

Palermo said she was shocked to see images showing work on the plaza floor to make way for a dancing fountain in front of the bandstand. She also questioned the installation of white spheres at the site.

City Ordinance 08-15-731, which was approved and signed by Gasataya when he was acting mayor in 2015, states that no structures or changes to existing structures within the plaza may be made without the express approval of the NHCP.

Palermo cited the National Cultural Heritage Act which provides legal protection for structures that qualify as important cultural properties (ICPs) and requires prior written approval for certain alterations or demolitions.
Under the law, ICPs, including structures at least 50 years old, cannot be altered or demolished without prior written approval from the NHCP.
The Bacolod Public Plaza will mark its 100th anniversary next year, Palermo said.
“Did the National Historical Commission grant prior written permission for changes or renovations at the Bacolod Public Plaza?” she asked.

Incidentally, the project is not the first controversy in Bacolod during Benitez’s term as mayor involving changes to culturally significant sites. Benitez and other city officials are also facing complaints before the Office of the Ombudsman over the demolition and rebuilding of the old city hall and the Fountain of Justice at the corner of Araneta and Luzuriaga streets.

Former city executive assistant Ernesto Pineda filed the complaints, which allege graft, procurement violations, technical malversation and the unauthorized demolition of the structures without clearance from the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP).
Pineda said the old city hall and Fountain of Justice were already considered important cultural properties (ICPs). The complaints remain pending before the Ombudsman.
The projects were awarded to Amigo Entertainment Technologies Incorporated (AETI), a company that specializes in audio, video, lighting and special-effects system integration.
Asked for copies of the blueprints, a female AETI staff member who declined to be identified said on Friday, October 2, that the documents were kept at the company’s head office in Taguig City.
She said AETI had the blueprints for the projects but could not provide a copy in Bacolod.

She also said the features visible at the Bacolod City Government Center grounds and public plaza, including the controversial white spheres scattered around the plaza, were included in the blueprints.

The assertion is significant because Benitez has said the finished project differs from what was originally proposed, while the spheres have themselves become a point of contention over the plaza’s design.

City Legal Officer Karol Joseph Chiu told Rappler on Monday, October 5, that the City Engineer’s Office has the blueprints for the two projects. He said what city hall does not have are the Bills of Quantities (BOQ).
“We have been asking TIEZA for the missing BOQ so we can have a clearer view of the projects, but so far, to no avail,” Chiu said.

A BOQ basically shows what work needs to be done on a project, how much of it is needed and how much it is expected to cost. It helps contractors prepare their bids and, once the contract is awarded, is used to determine how much the contractor should be paid for the work completed. It also breaks the project down into specific items so it is clear what work is being done, where it will be done and what it will cost.
The AETI staff member could not give a firm date for completion of the two projects.
“Only our bosses can speak on behalf of our company and status of work,” she said.

AETI is also the contractor for an P80-million aesthetic lighting project for the San Juanico Bridge in Samar and Leyte. Among its other projects is the aesthetic lighting of the Mount Samat Giant Cross in Pilar, Bataan. – Rappler.com

articles.title: France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests
articles.summary: Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some high schools after clashes between riot police and student protesters, France's education minister says.

blocks.text: Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said.
He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.
High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.
The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".

"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed.

"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".
On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors.

articles.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
articles.summary:
Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory

Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been…

blocks.text: Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.
The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.

Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”
The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.

blocks.caption: Egyptologist Flinders Petrie examining pottery, 1932. Photograph: Fox Photos/Getty Images

blocks.text: But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.

Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.

blocks.caption: The tomb of King Djer of Egypt, in Abydos. Photograph: Mike P Shepherd/Alamy

blocks.text: “This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century, but this is the first study to examine the human remains from the tombs themselves,” Campbell told the Guardian.
Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.
Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.

The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.

“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”
Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.

Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.

She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”

Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.

“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

articles.title: Ball in UK’s court: EU ambassador says Brussels will be ‘ready to engage‘ after country decides what it wants
articles.summary:
Jukka Salovaara, who served in London during Cool Britannia era, will be ‘very close’ to negotiations as Burnham government resets relations with EU

Jukka Salovaara, the newly…

blocks.text: Jukka Salovaara, the newly installed European Union ambassador to the UK, is likely to become a ubiquitous figure in national politics as the Andy Burnham government grapples with the question of its future relationship with the European Union.

Burnham has been clearer than his predecessor Keir Starmer in saying that what exists now is not working and that a full range of options, including rejoining, has to be on the table ahead of Labour’s next election manifesto.

Salovaara, aged 58, sees his role over the coming years as a “facilitator”, testing both sides like a good diplomat on what might fly and what will not work. He will not sit at the negotiating table, but he will be “very close to it”.

blocks.caption: Jukka Salovaara sees his role as a ‘facilitator’ testing both sides. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Everyone tells me my job is explaining London to Brussels and Brussels to London”. The UK, he says, remains “the European Union’s first and foremost partner”. When the two have made agreements, it has always been to “our mutual benefit”.

A former permanent secretary in Finland’s foreign ministry, who also served as his country’s ambassador to the UN, this is his first job with the European Commission, but not his first posting in the UK. As a young diplomat in the summer of 1996, he handled European affairs in London for Finland at the onset of Cool Britannia, just as Tony Blair was on the cusp of gaining power.

“The 1990s was such an optimistic time,” he says of that era. “World trade was growing. Interdependence was expected to provide security, and global norms and rules were strengthening. There was a feeling that globalisation and a rising tide would lift all boats.” The Labour government, he recalls, came “very close” to joining the euro.

blocks.caption: Tony Blair during the Cool Britannia era with German chancellor Gerhard Schröder at an EU summit in Cologne in 1999.  Photograph: Michael Jung/EPA

blocks.text: Since then, different ghosts have dominated UK politics. His office in Smith Square is just one floor up from that used by Margaret Thatcher in Conservative Central Office. The building was also a haunt for Nigel Farage when he was an MEP.

Burnham’s first EU summit is now pencilled in for November. Salovaara says issues such as how UK traders can avoid being caught up in the EU’s plans to prevent subsidised Chinese products flooding European markets will not be up for decision. The EU will not have completed its own legislative proposals by the time of the summit.

Salovaara says there are plenty of themes – food standards, linking the UK and EU carbon emissions trading scheme, youth mobility, and security – to keep the summit meaningful. On food, he points out: “When we have common standards we don’t need border checks. Nearly 60% of the UK’s food exports go to the EU market and 70% of the UK’s food imports come from the EU. Losing the red tape carries a lot of benefits.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Pro-EU protesters at Wesminster last summer.  Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Negotiations between the two sides over the details of any “youth experience scheme”, including the number of 18-to-30-year-olds able to participate and the rights to work and study they would enjoy, are still under way. The UK has initially offered 50,000 places a year, according to EU officials, but Brussels is pushing for 150,000.

As to the parameters of a future relationship, Europe must wait to see what the UK wants rather than setting out a collective opinion of its own, he says. “The ball is very much with the UK in terms of having this debate then looking at the options … and then the EU [will be] ready to engage.
“The approach up until now had been step by step, but this prime minister wants to assess all the options.”

But he acknowledges the difficulties. Charles Grant, the head of the Centre for European Reform, has said he cannot envisage Europe wanting the UK back as a full member unless there is a political consensus to rejoin inside the UK. Salovaara admits: “When you do something that is very fundamental it usually makes sense to have a strong consensus, but it is for the UK to decide if consensus must be proven through a further referendum.”

He runs through the other options in the regulatory staircase – such as joining the EU single market or customs union – but points out other novel, if as yet undefined blueprints are evolving, including associate membership, which is the option being proposed for Canada.

blocks.caption: Mark Carney, and Ursula von der Leyen in Strasbourg last month – could the UK follow in Canada’s footsteps and consider associate membership? Photograph: Pascal Bastien/AP

blocks.text: Another scheme – associated with Alexandre Adam, chief adviser to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – proposes that countries, including those locked in the Balkans EU accession waiting room, join the EU but without full rights of market access, which would be granted in time in return for commitments to democracy.

He points out that in the 1990s, European Economic Area countries such as Norway saw the relationship purely in economic terms, but have since come to see it as a more political relationship. “Look at how much Norway is integrated into what the EU does with Ukraine. Everyone is looking for a broader relationship with the EU.”

articles.title: Exiled separatist leader is likely to return to a very different Catalonia
articles.summary:
Nine years on from a failed independence push, former president Carles Puigdemont will find times have changed

After years of legal wrangling, Spain’s constitutional court is expected to…

blocks.text: After years of legal wrangling, Spain’s constitutional court is expected to remove the last obstacle to the return of the former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont after nearly nine years in exile this week.

Puigdemont fled in 2017 to avoid being jailed for his part in the failed and illegal independence push for which nine of his colleagues were imprisoned on sentences of up to 13 years, although all were released within three years.

If on 6 October the court decides, as expected, that the charge of misuse of public funds is covered by the amnesty law passed by the Spanish government in 2024, Puigdemont should be free to return without fear of arrest.
But will he come back like Lenin, leaping from the train in St Petersburg to galvanise the faltering revolution, or as yesterday’s man, the last of the Romanovs, bound for the dustbin of history?
Whether he returns in triumph or, as he departed, in the boot of a car, Catalonia today is very different from the place he left nine years ago.

Firstly, the political climate has changed beyond recognition. The fervour of mass demonstrations and constant conflict and provocation between Barcelona and Madrid has given way to a climate of cooperation.

Since 2024, the region has been governed by the Socialists’ party of Catalonia (PSC), the first time since 1980 that a non-nationalist party has been in charge. Led by Salvador Illa, Spain’s health minister during the Covid epidemic, it has ushered in an era of entente with Madrid, where the Socialist Workers’ party, to which the PSC serves as a regional section, is also in the driving seat.

Another change is that those young people who got fired up about independence are not only older now but face issues that are more pressing than sovereignty, principally jobs and housing. Wages are low, rents high and mortgages mostly out of reach. As a result, 82% of Catalonia’s 18- to 30-year-olds still live with their parents. On Friday Puigdemont’s Junts per Catalunya (Together for Catalonia) voted down the government’s progressive housing proposals, a move that won’t endear them to young Catalans, nor to their parents.

The other big change since 2017 is demographic. When Puigdemont went into exile, 13.8% of the Catalan population was foreign-born; the figure today is 18.7%. This shift is most marked in the capital, Barcelona, where 32% of residents are immigrants representing 118 nationalities, a figure that rises to 50% in the 12-35 age group.
For nationalists, this raises the question: who is a Catalan? Jordi Pujol, the Catalan president from 1980 to 2003, insisted that a Catalan was anyone who lived and worked in Catalonia.

Things are a little different now. Out of the disillusion of the independence movement has risen Aliança Catalana, a far-right nationalist party whose leader says “there isn’t room for everyone” in Catalonia.
Specifically, there would be no room for Muslims, not even those born in Spain, which by implication would include, for example, the Barcelona and Spain football star Lamine Yamal.

This has dragged Junts, traditionally the party of the Catalan bourgeoisie, to the right as those on the ethno-nationalist margins gravitate towards the unselfconsciously racist Aliança, whose positions on sovereignty are otherwise barely distinguishable from Junts’.
Over the past 25 years, Catalonia, and above all Barcelona, has gone from being a bicultural, bilingual Catalan-Spanish society to one that is multicultural and multilingual.
Puigdemont’s pitch is based on identity and a historical sense of grievance at Spain’s perceived abuse of and disdain for Catalonia, a sentiment shared by many, perhaps most, Catalans.
This ingrained sense of difference and grievance isn’t going away, but his vision may prove a harder sell than it was 10 years ago.

As demography changes, so does identity. Immigrants now make up nearly a fifth of the population, have their own identity issues and have no particular beef with Spain. As for independence, support never did reach 50%, and now hovers in the low 40s.

Besides, as people migrate in search of a better or perhaps a more interesting life, it is becoming increasingly likely that the parents of those living in Catalonia will be from different countries, and their sense of national identity is multiple or simply not that important.

Puigdemont’s lifelong dream is for Catalonia to take its place among the world’s independent nation states. Yet perhaps he is a man out of time and the nation state he craves, with its monocultural, monolingual badge of identity, has passed its sell-by date.

articles.title: All six passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
articles.summary: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.

blocks.text: Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.
On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.

"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."
The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.
On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.

The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).
Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.
"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.

"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."
Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.
FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).
Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.
"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"
The pilot's response was inaudible.
"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.
The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.
An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".
The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".
Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.
"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan upholds government claim on Manila property in ill-gotten wealth case
articles.summary: The commercial property in Paco, Manila, is registered under Taggat Industries owned by the late Alfonso Lim Sr. and his family

blocks.text: ANTI-GRAFT COURT. The Sandiganbayan in Quezon City.
Jansen Romero/Rappler
The commercial property in Paco, Manila, is registered under Taggat Industries owned by the late Alfonso Lim Sr. and his family

items: The Sandiganbayan court upheld the government's claim on a commercial property in Paco, Manila, linked to Taggat Industries in an ill-gotten wealth case from 1987.
The court ordered the transfer of the property's title to the Philippine government, affirming a previous decision from 2015 regarding the assets of Taggat Industries.
The ruling is supported by waivers from Alfonso Lim Jr. and the estate of Alfonso Lim Sr., relinquishing any claims over the properties involved in the case.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan has upheld the government’s claim on a commercial property in Paco, Manila, registered under corporate defendant Taggat Industries, Incorporated in a 1987 ill-gotten wealth case.

In a ruling dated September 30, the Sandiganbayan Second Division ordered the Register of Deeds of the City of Manila to transfer the title of the property in the name of the Philippine government, affirming the court’s December 14, 2015 decision on the properties and funds owned by Taggat Industries.
The Second Division sustained the government’s stand that the Paco, Manila property is already covered by the 2015 judgment.

“Accordingly, the Register of Deeds of Manila is directed upon compliance with applicable registration requirements, to cancel Transfer of Certificate of Title No. 78732 registered in the name of Taggat Industries, Inc. and to issue the corresponding transfer certificate of title in the name of the Republic of the Philippines,” the court ordered.

The Presidential Commission on Good Government filed Civil Case No. 0030 against alleged Marcos crony businessman Alfonso Lim Sr. in July 1987. Based on court records, Lim, who died in 1995, once held multiple timber license agreements (TLAs) under seven logging companies, covering 633,880 hectares.

The court’s 2015 decision to grant the government petition for the recovery and return of the ill-gotten wealth listed in “Annex A” of its complaint — which includes the Manila property — is based on two separate waivers executed by the late businessman’s son, Alfonso Lim Jr. and the estate of Alfonso Lim Sr.

In 2010, Lim Jr. issued a waiver and quitclaim informing the anti-graft court and the PCGG that in consideration for the dismissal of the ill-gotten wealth case, he was waiving “all his rights, interests, and participations, if any, and quits any and all claims he may have, if any, over any and all properties specified and particularly described in Annex ‘A’ of the Amended Complaint.”
He also ceded any claim over a Tagaytay City property.

After this, the estate of Alfonso D. Lim Sr. filed a separate manifestation, confirmation, waiver and quitclaim stating that it is “unequivocally and completely waives and surrenders in favor of the Republic of the Philippines any and all rights, claims, and interests it may have over the sequestered properties in the above-entitled case.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Supporters of jailed ex-PM Imran Khan march to Pakistan capital
articles.summary: Thousands have taken to the streets after talks between authorities and Khan's party ended in deadlock.

blocks.text: Thousands of supporters of Pakistan's jailed ex-prime minister Imran Khan are marching to the capital Islamabad as they call for his release.
Concerns over the 73-year-old's health have grown louder in recent months. His family claims he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
The cricket star-turned-politician, who faces charges in more than 100 cases, was jailed for 14 years over corruption last year. Khan said all the cases against him are politically motivated.
Even behind bars, he remains a force in Pakistani politics, and demonstrations in support for him have led to deadly violence and crackdowns in the past.
Sunday's march, which began in Lakki Marwat, a city 275km away from Islamabad, had paused for the night and is expected to resume around midday local time on Monday.
Originally scheduled for last week, it was postponed to allow for talks between the government and Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party but the talks ended in a deadlock.
Khan was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he has said are politically motivated.
Sohail Afridi, chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province ruled by PTI, expects that the march will make its way to a town about 80km (50 miles) west of Islamabad by Thursday.

"[By then] this movement will have reached every corner of the country and every square will have become a centre of activity," he said on Sunday, urging the people to "play an active role in the political process".
Authorities in Islamabad have stacked up shipping containers to block key access routes to the capital city.
The PTI said talks with government failed because authorities rejected the party's request for access to Khan so that its leaders could consult him on national and political issues.
The party also said it had demanded that Khan be given an immediate medical examination and treatment.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi meanwhile accused Afridi of "sabotaging" negotiations, saying the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had backed out of earlier commitments on counter-terrorism issues, according to Pakistan's local media reports.

In August, Khan was briefly transferred from jail to a state-run hospital for medical examination and treatment following complaints about his deteriorating health. The doctors later deemed him "medically fit".
The intervention was the most significant relief Khan has received from the courts since he was imprisoned in 2023 on corruption charges, which he says were politically motivated.
Khan's family and the PTI, however, criticised the authorities for defying a court order that he be examined by physicians at a specific private hospital.
On 20 September, Khan's sister Aleema Khanum was arrested in the eastern city of Lahore.
The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as the country's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
His jailing triggered large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging Khan be accorded proper medical care.

articles.title: US: FBI arrests woman accused of spying for China
articles.summary: A California woman was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport, just before departing for China, with the US officials accusing her of spying on Taiwan's president's son.

image.caption: Wanying Z., who was arrested by the FBI, was also known as HeatherImage: via REUTERS

blocks.text: US officials announced on Sunday that a woman had been arrested by the FBI and accused of spying for China in the United States.
Wanying Z., 34, of Irvine, California, was detained at at Los Angeles International Airport ahead of a scheduled flight to China.
She faces charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent.

The woman "traveled to Seattle in 2025 and, at the direction of (People's Republic of China) officials, surveilled a close relative of a Taiwanese government official, sending photos, videos and license plate information to those officials," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said in an online post.
He added that Z. "coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection."
The woman is due to appear before a Los Angeles federal court on Monday, Essayli wrote.

blocks.caption: Wanying Z. was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport before she was set to fly to ShanghaiImage: via REUTERS

blocks.text: Who was the alleged target of surveillance?

The FBI said Z. was spying on a son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te. While the US agency did not provide the target's name, they later shared a New York Post report identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, who is reportedly a US resident.
In an X post, FBI Director Kash Patel celebrated the arrest, warning foreign adversaries that "America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations."
"Allegedly surveil a foreign leader's family on US soil for the PRC — and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening," Patel added.
Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party advocate for Taiwan's distinct identity from China. Their statements often irritate Beijing, which considers the island Chinese territory.
While Washington does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, the United States is the island's most important international supporter and supplier of weapons.

articles.title: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
articles.summary: The president named his national intelligence chief as the taskforce's head as worries over AI grow.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump says he has created a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.
It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".
Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact.

"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.

Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research, Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.
It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as the US national intelligence director in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.
On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.
The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.

In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.
"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.
The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.

On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding, arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems.

Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI.
"SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote.
The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war.
Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump.

articles.title: PNP requires gun vault photo for new, renewed firearm licenses
articles.summary: After school shootings, PNP adds gun storage proof to license applications.

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 11:37am
Sport gun enthusiasts undergo firearms training under the guidance of range officers at the ARMSCOR firing range in Marikina City on June 27, 2026
The STAR / Walter Bollozos

MANILA, Philippines — Private individuals applying for or renewing a license to own and possess firearms must now submit a photo showing their firearm storage facility as part of tighter gun safekeeping requirements taking effect Monday, October 5.

In an October 1 advisory, the Philippine National Police's Firearms and Explosives Office said applicants must declare that proper storage and safety measures are available for their firearms before their License to Own and Possess Firearms application can be approved.
The FEO has revised its application forms for both new and renewing license holders to reflect the requirement.

"Please be informed that effective October 5, 2026, the Firearms and Explosives Office Form No. 1 (Revision - September 2026) and Firearms and Explosives Office Form No. 2 (Revision - September 2026) application forms shall be used for all new and renewal LTOPF transactions," the advisory read.
Applicants must submit a photo of themselves with their firearm vault or storage container, which must be secured by a lock and key, along with the other documentary requirements.

The requirement to safely store firearms itself is not new. Existing firearms regulations already require holders of Type 1 to Type 5 licenses to keep their guns in a vault or container secured by lock and key or other appropriate security measures.
The new FEO policy, however, adds documentary proof of compliance to the application process.
Stricter safekeeping
The stricter requirement comes after a series of fatal school shootings this year linked to minors' use of firearms licensed to adults.

In the June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, one of the two minor suspects used a Glock pistol issued to his aunt, a police officer. The officer later told a Senate inquiry that the gun had been kept in a locked plastic locker rather than a safety vault.

In August, a student who carried out a shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University used two firearms belonging to his father, a Customs police officer. The Bureau of Customs confirmed that one was agency-issued while the other was his licensed personal firearm.

A third school shooting in Banga, South Cotabato, on September 18 involved a licensed firearm owned by the shooter's father, a Department of Education employee. Authorities said the firearm had been kept in a vault that the student was able to open or break into.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla had earlier proposed allowing police to inspect the homes of licensed gun owners to verify proper storage, arguing that firearm ownership in the Philippines is a privilege that carries responsibilities. He later clarified that the proposed inspections would require gun owners to consent through a waiver and receive prior notice.
The PNP has also said it would tighten firearms safekeeping rules for police personnel following the school shooting incidents.

articles.title: How Niña Sandejas captured nu-metal band Greyhoundz’ legacy in print
articles.summary: Through her lens and in her own words, renowned music photographer Niña Sandejas tells the story of iconic band Greyhoundz and the sub-genre 'kupaw' in her first book

blocks.text: Niña Sandejas had always wanted to write a book.

She was only seven years old when she realized that this had become a dream of hers — and even if, for the longest time, she didn’t really know what she’d write about, she continued to hold onto that goal in the years to come.

But as life would have it, her first work as a published author would not come until decades later, as an almost entirely different creative endeavor found her first: music photography. Her command of the lens and ability to capture the moving parts of live music performances would help her build a reputation as a prominent creative.
Still, Sandejas had turned out to be on the right path.

If somebody were to create a photobook about nu-metal band Greyhoundz, who would be better suited for the job? Someone who understands the delicate push and pull between pictures and words, it seems, and that someone is Sandejas.

It took the seasoned music photographer, now a published author, around 10 years to figure out what she wanted to say and tell the stories of Reg Rubio, Audie Avenido, Niño Avenido, TJ Brillantes, Allen Cudal, and Greyhoundz as a whole in print.

“That was actually my default from day one,” Sandejas said about taking on both the role of the photographer and the writer simultaneously. “I journal a lot, and I used to write recaps of shows and nights out on my old blog. Sometimes I’d forget because I’d think, well, the photographs are there, they’ll explain it. But they don’t always.”

“I think doing both the writing and the photography meant I could let one fill in what the other couldn’t. Sometimes the photograph already says everything and I should leave it alone. Other times I know the story around the photograph, and that changes what you’re looking at.”

The photobook, published under Sandejas’ independent press, alt164 Press, is just over 400 pages of writing and photography. Its pages come with golden edges, and the book itself is simply titled Greyhoundz, almost as if it is up to you to accept the invitation into Greyhoundz’ crazy world, as told by Sandejas.

blocks.caption: NIÑA SANDEJAS. Music photographer and now-published author Niña Sandejas holds a copy of the Greyhoundz photobook published under alt164 Press. Photo by Con Lauro

blocks.text: “The Greyhoundz book itself only has a little over 5,000 words. It’s still very much a photobook, and photographs are my strongest language here. The writing was there to give context when context was necessary, but part of making the book was also learning when to shut up and let the photographs do the work,” she said.

Yet completely capturing the legacy of a band that defies the bounds between metal and hip-hop appears to be a daunting task. It’s one thing to take photos at a Greyhoundz gig, but it’s completely different to dive into their world, from coming face to face with fans in a sweaty open-air venue to winding down backstage after an electrifying set.

blocks.caption: GREYHOUNDZ. Photo by Niña Sandejas

blocks.text: It was the latter that gave Sandejas the ability to truly get to know the men of Greyhoundz through the years. It wasn’t only seeing them in action, but also the casual conversations she’d have with each member that shaped the Greyhoundz book into what it is now.

“That’s kind of how I work anyway. If I stay with an artist long enough, I remember the conversations and little things that strike me as interesting, and over time I get a better sense of who they are and what might be worth remembering about them,” she explained.

Take the chapter about bassist Niño Avenido for instance. It starts with two simple, yet telling sentences about pretty much everything you needed to know about Avenido’s drive as an artist: “It takes two hands to play bass. Niño managed to break both.”

blocks.caption: BASSIST. Greyhoundz’ bassist Niño Avenido. Photo by Niña Sandejas

blocks.text: Sandejas lays out anecdotes about Avenido’s injuries that made it difficult for him to play normally, and his stubbornness that allowed him to rack up several “Bassist of the Year” awards. It’s these kinds of moments that bring out the most meaningful stories, and Sandejas had a front-row seat to it all.

“That access eventually becomes a responsibility. I know I’m married to Niño now, but we weren’t married until years after I started photographing Greyhoundz. And I think you have to be genuinely interested in people beyond what makes them notable. It’s easy to fall into this collector’s mindset where photographing somebody becomes a benchmark like, okay, I got that person, next. I’m much more interested in what the whole body of work becomes when you stay,” she told Rappler.
What happens, though, if the individual you are meant to profile has long passed?

It would be remiss not to have a section about Greyhoundz guitarist Allen Cudal, who died in 2004. Even though Sandejas had never gotten the chance to meet him, her husband, Avenido, assured her that they would have gotten along.
“I had to be careful not to write about him as if I knew him personally. Most of my understanding of Allen came from the people who loved him and from what he left behind,” Sandejas shared.

“So I wrote about his presence through his guitar, which is literally just outside my room. Musicians develop these incredibly personal relationships with their instruments. They name them, they wear them down, and I do believe they leave some kind of energetic imprint on them. It was a little spooky because I could see the guitar from where I was working and almost feel its presence while I was writing the whole thing.”

When you’ve spent years documenting a band’s journey and eventually embed yourself into their everyday chaos, it becomes all the more difficult to choose which parts of them are worth making the final cut. The thousands of photographs Sandejas had taken of Greyhoundz each came with a story of their own, after all.

blocks.caption: A full-page spread of drummer TJ Brillantes. Photo by Niña Sandejas

blocks.text: “So I had to keep asking myself what each photograph or story was doing there. Does it move something forward? Does it tell you something you wouldn’t otherwise know? Will anybody care about this decades from now? That was probably the hardest part: accepting that making an archive doesn’t mean putting everything in. Sometimes preserving the story means deciding what you can afford to leave out,” she said.
More importantly, however, it was the broader question of why Greyhoundz’ story deserved to be told that laid the groundwork for Sandejas’ book.

“I think Greyhoundz has a very universal message about survival, endurance, breaking barriers, and earning the respect of a scene through the music itself. You can take that lesson out of music entirely and apply it to almost anyone trying to keep going through whatever life throws at them,” said Sandejas about what she wanted people to understand about Greyhoundz.
“Bands have lifespans, and Greyhoundz had already experienced the death of a band member only seven years into their career. That’s something not every band survives, but they kept going.

And I think that persistence became part of what kupaw meant too. It started as a sound in their music and eventually became a name for the whole subgenre they helped pioneer, but there was also a feeling around it — the aggression, the community, the humor, the loyalty, the release you felt when you were inside that scene. It was an outlet for many of us who were there, and this book allows people a glimpse into that world,” she added.

blocks.caption: GREYHOUNDZ. Photo by Niña Sandejas

blocks.text: Whether or not you were already an avid listener, you will get to the last page of the book understanding why the group became as iconic as they are in the Filipino music scene. And it’s through Sandejas’ masterful command of both the lens, and in effect, the pen that makes space for that to happen.
Truly, then, you dunno what’s comin’ at ya. – Rappler.com

The book is priced at P4,990 and may be purchased from www.alt164.press and in select Fully Booked branches: Bonifacio High Street, SM City Sta. Rosa, SM Baguio, Ayala Malls Central Bloc Cebu, and SM Lanang Davao.

items: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes the benefits of AI outweigh the risks and advocates for broad public access to the technology.

The debate over AI development and regulation is intensifying, with contrasting views on the pace of advancement and the associated risks.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public

“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman said in an interview with Politico’s technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation, adding: “I think there’s a lot of daylight.”

“I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, ‘This technology is going to get so powerful, and it’s so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'” Altman said.
He called that “a completely unacceptable trade-off” that runs counter to the “lighter-touch regulatory stance” backed by OpenAI.

“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen,'” Altman said. “Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff.”
Altman’s remarks come amid a growing debate within the AI industry over the pace of development and the risks posed by increasingly capable systems.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September published an essay calling on the industry to slow down to “pace the frontier,” a stance that Altman publicly endorsed. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, saying the people building AI believe it “could kill us all by the end of the decade.

blocks.caption: Anthropic warns AI may pose ‘existential risks to humanity’ in IPO filing

blocks.text: Reuters reported in September that Anthropic warned that, despite AI’s potential benefits, the technology can sometimes act in ways that run counter to its makers’ intentions and penetrate other companies’ systems. The company said advanced models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviors,” including attempts to “resist shutdown,” “conceal or manipulate information,” or generate outputs that could be interpreted as “coercive, deceptive, or manipulative.”

However, US President Donald Trump has largely dismissed calls for new restrictions, arguing they would make it harder for American companies to compete with Chinese rivals. He has repeatedly said existing law enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, provide sufficient safeguards and that no new rules are needed. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Missed opportunity': Law prof faults prosecution's Sara property presentation
articles.summary: He says documents should support its explanation of the questioned Samal property.

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 10:11am

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecutors missed a chance to clearly establish whether properties registered to Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband were omitted from her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth, a law professor said.

Adonis Gabriel, a professor at the San Beda University College of Law, said prosecutors should have presented the couple's relevant property titles together and compared them with Duterte's declared assets.

"With all due respect to the prosecution, nagkulang ang prosecution sa paglalahad nila ng testimonya ng mga tao natin sa [Land Registration Authority]," Gabriel said in Filipino in an interview with dzBB on October 2.
(With all due respect to the prosecution, it fell short in presenting the testimony of the Land Registration Authority personnel.)

In particular, Gabriel referred to the October 1 testimony of the registers of deeds of Davao City and Samal under Article II of Duterte's impeachment case, which mainly accuses her of unexplained wealth and failure to divest from business interests.

The witnesses identified land titles, deeds of sale and tax declarations for properties registered to Duterte's husband, lawyer Manases Carpio. Both repeatedly said they could not determine whether the properties matched entries in Duterte's SALNs.

Gabriel said prosecutors should have presented all relevant titles and compared them with the properties declared in Duterte's SALNs. Any registered property left unmatched, he said, could then have been clearly identified as potentially undeclared.
"Ang ginawa ng prosecution, inilahad lamang nila ang isang titulo ng isang property," Gabriel said. (What they just did was to state the title of one property.)

He noted that SALNs do not require property title numbers, making a direct comparison based on the title number alone impossible. The form instead requires identifying details such as the property's location and type, assessed and fair market values, acquisition year and mode, and acquisition cost.

"Sa paglalahad ng mga testigo sa korte, para ka ring naglalahad ng kuwento sa ating mga hukom. Sa paglalahad ng kuwento, dapat maipakita mo nang malinaw iyong gusto mong impormasyon na lumabas," Gabriel said. (Presenting witnesses in court is like telling a story to the judges. You must clearly show the information you want to establish.)
Gabriel said the prosecution fell short because it did not make that comparison sufficiently clear.
"So that's a missed opportunity for the prosecution dahil hindi nila nailahad nang malinaw na may mga properties doon sa SALN ng ating bise presidente na hindi naisama," he said.
(So that's a missed opportunity for the prosecution because they were not able to clearly establish that there were properties not included in the vice president's SALN.)
Undisclosed documents
Gabriel said Duterte's camp also needed to substantiate its explanation for a questioned property in Samal.

The defense said during cross-examination that a property appeared in Duterte's 2013 SALN, while the property questioned by prosecutors was transferred to her in 2018. The defense's theory, Gabriel said, was that the property had been acquired through a contract to sell beginning in 2013, with ownership formally transferred in 2018.
Gabriel said the defense should produce the contract to sell, payment records, tax documents and records of improvements to establish that the earlier SALN entry referred to the same property.
"Kaya ang inaasahan ko sa ating bise presidente bilang public officer, kailangan niya ring patunayan na iyong property na hinahanap ninyo ay ito iyong nakarehistro noong 2013," Gabriel said.
(What I expect of the vice president as a public officer is that she also substantiate that the property being questioned is the one recorded in 2013.)
Gabriel said a general denial would not be enough and stressed the transparency expected of public officials.
"Bilang public officer, kailangan maging transparent tayo. Iyan ang purpose ng statement of assets, liabilities, and net worth," he said.
(As public officers, we need to be transparent. That is the purpose of the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.)

After presenting records on real properties and firearms last week, prosecutors are moving into Duterte and Carpio's financial records on Monday, October 5. Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura has been called to testify as the prosecution seeks to compare financial transactions with the couple's declared assets and net worth.

articles.title: Jane Doe at centre of Cornell rape case targeted with threats, her lawyer says
articles.summary: The woman who has alleged she was drugged and raped by ‌Cornell University students has been the target of threats, her lawyer said on Sunday.

image.caption: Students walk past the entrance of Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Thursday. (Lauren Petracca/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
The woman who has alleged she was drugged and raped by ‌Cornell University students has been the target of threats, her lawyer said on Sunday.
Cornell under scrutiny following outcry over university's handling of allegations

Thomas Giuffra, who represents the woman identified as Jane Doe, told CNN that people have threatened to silence or harm her if she does not withdraw her civil lawsuit alleging that several members of a Cornell fraternity drugged and ​raped her in 2024.
"She's received multiple threats," Giuffra said on CNN's State ​of the Union, adding that he had also been threatened.

"I'm not afraid of these people," he said. "But the threats, the abuse to protect what's going on, the status quo — these guys are ​disgusting. They should stay in their mother's basement and stay out of the world."

The identity of ⁠Jane Doe has become ⁠part of the fevered online conversation surrounding the case. Women ‌on social media have been posting #IamJaneDoe in solidarity with the accuser and to counter some who have sought to publicly name her.
Advocate calls for 'overhaul' of student groups to address harms on campuses like Cornell

Michael Tracey, an independent journalist and commentator, posted on Friday what he said was the accuser's name, which Reuters was unable to verify, before quickly deleting it, saying his point had been ⁠made.

He has expressed sympathy for the accused men over what he says is the harassment they have faced and described his effort to name the Cornell accuser as journalistic diligence protected under the U.S. Constitution as free speech.

articles.title: US pulls bombers out of UK's Fairford airbase after arrests
articles.summary: Following a suspected terrorist plot targeting the UK's Fairford airbase, the US Air Force withdrew all its B-1 planes from the site.

image.caption: US B-1 bombers stationed at RAF Fairford were used for strikes against IranImage: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A week after several men were detained at the Royal Air Force (RAF) base in the UK's Fairford on suspicion of planning terrorist attacks, a Pentagon official announced that the United States had removed its B-1 bombers from the base northwest of London.
On Sunday, aircraft monitoring sites showed the B-1 aircraft flying out of the UK base.

"While operational security precluded us from ​confirming the movement of our assets and forces ​in real-time, ‌we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home ‌stations in the United States," a Pentagon spokesman wrote ‌in ​a statement.

A dozen B-1 bombers had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the British airbase used by the US. London previously allowed the Pentagon to fly sorties out of Fairford against Iranian missile sites which were threatening ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
UK releases air base plot suspects
What do we know about the suspected plot
Last Sunday, police were called to a base in southwest England after a local farmer reported a group of men in several vans engaging in "suspicious" activity.

Investigators blocked off the area and called in the bomb disposal teams. However, no explosives were found in the vehicles. Later, the five British nationals arrested in connection to the incident were released on bail.
US President Donald Trump voiced his disappointment over their release.
On Wednesday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that Britain had "strong indications" that Iran was involved in a suspected plot targeting the base.
Iran dismissed the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran to discuss the issue.

articles.title: One Nation to establish headquarters in multimillion dollar Brisbane office bought by Gina Rinehart
articles.summary: Barnaby Joyce defends move, saying party will lease space off mining billionaire’s company at commercial rates Barnaby Joyce says there’s no conflict of interest between One Nation and mining…

blocks.text: Barnaby Joyce says there’s no conflict of interest between One Nation and the mining billionaire Gina Rinehart after it was revealed that Australia’s richest woman had bought a new multimillion-dollar Brisbane office for the minor party to lease.
The One Nation MP said the party’s national head office would pay the market rate to Rinehart’s company to rent the space, claiming there would be no mate’s rates.
“I don’t live in her [Gina’s] pocket,” Joyce told News24. “It’s her building, it’s her lease. We’re leasing it off her at commercial rates.
“If … we’ve got an individual who’s got money, they should be allowed to spend it as they see fit.”

Rinehart’s property investment company Hanrine finalised the purchase of the three-storey office in the Brisbane suburb of Spring Hill last week, Queensland property titles confirm, and as first reported by The Australian newspaper on Monday.
It’s believed to be valued at about $8m, according to The Australian. Property data shows it was last sold for $2.4m in 2003.
The building has two floors with 10 parking spaces at its lower level. The sale ad boasts it comes with a “large top-floor balcony with sweeping city views”.
Joyce said One Nation would pay for the office space out of the party’s “wallet”.

A spokesperson for Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting said: “Hancock Prospecting holds a range of commercial property, and this building is one of them. Hancock is not providing free or discounted space to any outside tenant, political or otherwise.”
Guardian Australia has contacted One Nation for a response.

Pauline Hanson’s relationship with Rinehart has been the subject of the Guardian’s new podcast about the party, The Populist, which detail numerous instances when the Queensland senator and the party she leads have received gifts or benefits.
after newsletter promotion

Guardian Australia revealed last month that Hanson and Joyce stayed overnight at Rinehart’s $20m Brisbane mansion in April after fundraising events held for One Nation. On one occasion, Joyce conducted a live television interview with Channel Seven’s Sunrise program from a room that appears to be a bedroom in Rinehart’s home.
Joyce told News24 on Monday he hadn’t spoken to Rinehart in six months.
The reporting also revealed that Hanson has been using one of Rinehart’s bodyguards for her personal security.
The man, who has been seen escorting Hanson in Perth and Canberra, has been one of Rinehart’s closest bodyguards for more than a decade.

One Nation has also committed multiple breaches of Senate rules, with the party failing to declare a number of flights gifted by Hancock Prospecting to Hanson going back to August last year, including flights to attend a Conservative Political Action Conference in Florida and Donald Trump’s Great Gatsby-themed Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago.
Hanson has said she considers Rinehart an unofficial policy adviser to her and One Nation.

“My policy on pensioners being able to work unlimited hours and without losing their pension or healthcare card came from Mrs Rinehart,” Hanson told ABC radio in Perth in June. “And I think that’s great. I listen to anyone who brings good policy to me.
“I consider her a friend and I’m very … grateful for her support. She’s an Australian identity, she’s one of the highest taxpayers in the country.”

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Former Bachelor star Sam Wood charged with domestic violence
articles.summary: Fitness influencer, 46, faces court on Monday after his arrest in Noosa at the weekend The fitness influencer and reality TV star Sam Wood has been charged in Queensland with domestic violence…

blocks.text: The fitness influencer and reality TV star Sam Wood has been charged in Queensland with domestic violence offences.
The personal trainer and star of the third season of reality TV show The Bachelor was charged on Sunday and spent the weekend in police custody after an alleged incident on Saturday night.

Mark Watkin, acting CEO of 28 Group, now the parent company of fitness business 28 by Sam Wood, said in a statement on Monday that the company was “shocked and saddened by the matters involving Sam Wood.”
“We have zero tolerance for domestic violence. While the matter is under investigation and before the court, Sam is on indefinite leave from his duties,” Watkin said.
“Our thoughts are with the family and anyone in the community affected by domestic violence.”

A statement posted simultaneously to Wood’s personal Instagram account and that of his wife, Snezana Wood, on Monday morning, said: “This is a difficult time for all of us, we are working through this as a family and are thoroughly co-operating with authorities.”
On Sunday, Queensland police confirmed they had arrested a 46-year-old Victorian man and charged him with domestic violence offences.
The arrest came after officers attended a Noosa address about 9pm on Saturday night after receiving reports of alleged domestic violence.
The man has been charged with assaulting occasioning bodily harm (domestic violence) and strangulation in a domestic setting, police said.
The alleged victim or victims have not been identified.
Wood was refused bail and was expected to appear in Maroochydore magistrates court on Monday.
The personal trainer shot to national prominence when he starred as the eponymous Bachelor in the third season of the reality TV show franchise in 2015.
He met Snezana Markoski when she was a contestant on the show. The couple married in 2018 in Byron Bay. They have four daughters including one from Markoski’s previous relationship.
Wood owns and runs personal training studio The Woodshed in Brighton East, Melbourne.
He built a fitness and nutrition business, 28 by Sam Wood, off the back of his increased profile from The Bachelor, eventually selling the company in 2022 for $71.2m.

Over the past year, the Australian Taxation Office has been pursuing Wood for alleged unpaid tax debts, reported to be in excess of $7 million. Case listings noted in August that a settlement had been reached, with the case dismissed in September.
Wood has recently launched a telehealth-based weight-loss platform aimed at middle-aged women, called Ollo for Women.
Guardian Australia has approached businesses connected to Wood for comment.
